paragraphs: I've worked Lamorinda and the surrounding Contra Costa communities long enough to recognize a well-cared-for home the moment I see one, and 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. caught my attention right away. The combination of a single-story footprint, a saltwater pool, and that kind of meticulous top-to-bottom update work is genuinely uncommon at any price point, let alone in West Alamo. When the listing came off market after just 22 days without a sale, I wanted to understand why, and I think I have a clear picture.

Twenty-two days is short enough that most sellers assume the market simply wasn't ready, but in my experience that window is exactly when the right strategy matters most. At $917 per square foot on a 1949 home, even one with serious upgrades, buyers need to feel the full case before they'll commit at that number. The listing description threw a lot at the wall, and some of the strongest selling points, the smart-home lighting, the commercial-grade range, the indoor-outdoor pool setting, got buried in a list of features rather than being built into a narrative that connected the home's character to what West Alamo buyers are actually looking for. The home has real substance. The marketing didn't quite build the brief for it.

I've put together a short packet for you that walks through the three specific friction points I see in the listing history, a side-by-side look at where $917 per square foot sits in the Alamo market today, and the approach I'd take to relaunch this home with a strategy designed around its actual strengths rather than a standard MLS playbook.

If you're already working with a real estate agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside with my best wishes. If you're not, I'd genuinely enjoy a short conversation about what a relaunch could look like.

exec_summary.headline: A Meticulously Updated West Alamo Single-Story  -  and a Listing That Didn't Build the Case for It
exec_summary.p1: 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. offers something that is genuinely hard to find in Alamo: a fully updated single-story home on a private lot with a saltwater pool, smart-home systems, a commercial-grade kitchen, and mature landscaping that creates real indoor-outdoor living. The 2,178 square feet of living space is sensibly distributed for both everyday use and entertaining, and the scope of recent improvements, new flooring, new exterior and interior paint, new pavers, Lutron smart-lighting throughout, a resurfaced driveway, and a thermostatically-controlled fireplace in the primary suite, signals a move-in-ready home that a busy professional or relocating family can step into without a project list.
exec_summary.p2: The listing history doesn't match those fundamentals. At $1,998,000 and $917 per square foot on a 1949 footprint, this home sits at the upper edge of the Alamo standard tier and needs marketing that builds the case for that number clearly and early. The listing description leads with caps-heavy fragments and a sequential feature list rather than a story, and it never frames the specific combination of location, condition, and lifestyle that separates this property from newer construction at a lower price per square foot. Buyers comparing options at this level need to feel why the number is right before they schedule a showing. That story was there. It just wasn't told.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to do one thing above all else: make the premium legible. That means building the narrative around what this specific home delivers, single-story living, a private pool setting, smart-home infrastructure, and a West Alamo address with top schools, in a way that arms buyers with the rationale to justify $917 per square foot against every other option they're considering.

forensics.title: Friction #1: Narrative Failure  -  A Strong Home Described as a Feature List
forensics.body: The listing description for 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. reads as an inventory of improvements rather than a case for the home. All-caps fragments like 'WEST ALAMO w/TOP ALAMO SCHOOLS' and 'SALT WATER POOL' pull attention without grounding the buyer in the experience of living there. Details worth real money, the Lutron Casita smart-lighting system, the commercial-grade gas range, the thermostatically-controlled fireplace in the primary suite, are dropped mid-list rather than anchored to the lifestyle a buyer at $1,998,000 is actually imagining. At this price point, buyers are comparing carefully, and a description that reads like a form submission gets scrolled past. This home had a story worth telling, and it still does.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's listing remarks are written the way a great buyer's agent describes a home to a client, specific, sequential, and emotionally grounded. Paired with Zillow Showcase placement, the narrative reaches buyers at the exact moment they're deciding whether to schedule a showing.

forensics.title: Friction #2: Premium Not Justified in Marketing  -  $917/sqft on a 1949 Footprint
forensics.body: At $917 per square foot, 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. is priced at the top of the Alamo standard tier and at the entry point of the premium tier. That number is defensible, the scope of updates, the saltwater pool, the smart-home infrastructure, the single-story layout on a private lot, absolutely support it. But buyers comparing this home against newer construction at $850 to $950 per square foot need to understand specifically what they're getting here that they can't find elsewhere at this price. Without a marketing approach that builds that case visually and narratively before a showing, price-conscious buyers move on before they ever walk through the door.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's 3D Matterport tour lets buyers walk every room of the home from anywhere, at any time, so they arrive at a showing already understanding the floor plan, the scale, and the finish level, with the confidence to justify the number before they ever step inside.

forensics.title: Friction #3: Visual Story Never Told  -  A Saltwater Pool Setting Left to Imagination
forensics.body: The backyard at 1489 Sunnybrook Rd., irrigated lush landscaping, a saltwater pool, private fencing, and new pavers, is exactly the kind of California indoor-outdoor setting that moves buyers in the Alamo market. That setting lives or dies on photography. Standard MLS angles rarely capture the relationship between a pool, the surrounding landscape, and the home itself in a way that communicates the lifestyle rather than just documenting the amenity. A buyer scrolling listings at $1,998,000 needs to feel the backyard before they schedule a showing. Without the right visual, a saltwater pool registers as a checkbox rather than a reason to buy.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour places the lot, the pool setting, the landscaping, and the street presence in full aerial context, giving online buyers the spatial understanding that ground photography simply cannot replicate.

positioning_table.verdict: At $917/sqft versus a benchmark range of $850-$950/sqft, this home sits near the upper end of that range. At $917 per square foot, 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. sits at the upper edge of the Alamo standard tier, a number the home's condition and amenities can support, but one that required marketing built to make the case. The full-scope renovation, the saltwater pool setting, and the smart-home infrastructure together justify the position, but buyers at this level need that argument laid out for them clearly and early. The gap here was not in the home. It was in the strategy.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Building the Narrative That Earns $917 Per Square Foot
pillars.body: At this price point in Alamo, buyers are doing serious homework before they schedule a showing. The listing remarks for 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. need to lead with the experience of living here, single-story ease, a private pool setting, a smart-home kitchen, a primary suite that functions as a real retreat, not a sequential list of upgrades. BrightWork rewrites the story from the buyer's perspective, so the number feels earned before they ever visit. The right narrative doesn't just describe a home. It makes the case for it.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Showing the Backyard the Way It Deserves to Be Seen
pillars.body: The saltwater pool, the irrigated landscaping, the new pavers and fencing, these are premium selling points that require premium visual treatment. A Sky Tour places the entire outdoor setting in context, capturing the lot position, the pool, and the relationship between the backyard and the home in a way that no ground-level photograph can. Buyers who have already experienced the backyard visually arrive at showings prepared to fall in love with it in person, not discovering it for the first time at the front door.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Reaching the Right Buyer Before They Find Something Else
pillars.body: The buyer for 1489 Sunnybrook Rd. is likely a busy professional or relocating family, possibly coming from San Francisco or the East Bay, who is shopping Alamo online before committing to a weekend of showings. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns put this home in front of those buyers while they are still in the research phase, before they have narrowed their list to homes from agents who waited for them to come to the MLS. A 22-day window with no sale is a distribution problem as much as anything else. The right buyer was out there. The listing just didn't reach them.
